Pluck the open A string on a guitar, and a tuner will tell you it's 110 Hz, meaning the string swings up and down 110 times every second. This count is called the *frequency*. 

But run the same sound through a spectrum analyzer, a tool that splits a sound into its separate frequencies, and it turns out that a single note contains several frequencies at once: not just 110 Hz, but 220, 330 Hz, and so on. The lowest of these, 110 Hz, is the *fundamental*, and it sets the pitch you hear. The rest, at whole-number multiples of it, are the *harmonics*, and are colors that set instruments apart.

This naturally raises two questions:

1. **Why are the harmonics whole-number multiples of the fundamental?** 

2. **Why can a plucked string produce so many harmonics, instead of just the fundamental?** 

We will start with the first question, as its answer will be helpful for the second question.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import Audio, display

plt.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "animation.embed_limit": 40})
integrate = getattr(np, "trapezoid", None) or np.trapz  

L = 1.0        # string length
h  = 1.0       # how far you pull the string
f1 = 110.0     # open A string, in Hz
T  = 1 / f1    # one period, about 9.1 ms
x  = np.linspace(0, L, 1001)
fs = 44100     # audio sample rate

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

L, f1 = 1.0, 110
COLORS = ["#2F6FDE", "#E8833A"]  # alternate per wavelength: blue, orange

def draw_string(ax, k, nodes):
    """One panel: k half-wavelengths on a string fixed at 0 and L."""
    lam = 2 * L / k
    for j, x0 in enumerate(np.arange(0, L, lam)):  # one segment per wavelength
        x = np.linspace(x0, min(x0 + lam, L), 300)
        ax.plot(x, np.sin(k * np.pi * x / L), color=COLORS[j % 2], lw=2.5, solid_capstyle="butt")
    ax.plot(nodes, np.zeros_like(nodes), "ko", ms=5, zorder=3, clip_on=False)
    for xv in (0, L):
        ax.axvline(xv, color="gray", lw=1.5, clip_on=False)  # fixed ends
    ax.axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.8, ls="--")              # rest position
    ax.set(ylim=(-1.7, 1.7), yticks=[-1, 0, 1])
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
    ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)


def finish(fig, axes):
    """Shared x-axis, labels and legend."""
    for ax in axes[:-1]:
        ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
        ax.tick_params(bottom=False)
    axes[-1].set_xticks([0, L / 2, L], ["0", "L/2", "L"])
    axes[-1].set_xlabel("position along the string", fontsize=9)
    fig.supylabel("displacement", fontsize=9)
    handles = [Line2D([], [], color=c, lw=2.5, label=f"{o} wavelength")
               for c, o in zip(COLORS, ["1st", "2nd"])]
    handles.append(Line2D([], [], color="k", marker="o", ls="", ms=5, label="node"))
    fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="upper center", ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=9)
```

## A rope example

Before tackling harmonics head on, it may be helpful to think of a guitar string as a rope tied to a post, with you holding the other end and shaking it. 

If you shake it at just the right rhythm, the whole rope swings as one big loop. Shake twice as often and it snaps into two loops, with a point in the middle that stays still. Three times as often gives three loops. At any rates in between, no clean pattern builds up and the rope just jiggles. How often you shake is a frequency, and these special frequencies are exactly the fundamental and its harmonics.

In physics, these patterns are called *modes*, and the points that never move, including the two ends, are called *nodes*. An up-loop followed by a down-loop makes one full wave, and its length is called the *wavelength* $\lambda$. So one loop is half a wavelength.

The figure below shows each mode as a snapshot. In reality, each loop keeps flipping between up and down, while the dots stay perfectly still.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The first four modes of a string with a fundamental $f_1$ of 110 Hz. The dots are nodes, and $n$ is the number of loops. Each color marks one full wavelength, so at $n = 1$ the string holds only half a wavelength."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(7, 6.5), sharex=True)
for n, ax in enumerate(axes, start=1):
    draw_string(ax, n, nodes=np.linspace(0, L, n + 1))
    ax.text(1.04, 0.5, f"n = {n}\n{n * f1} Hz", transform=ax.transAxes, va="center", fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_xlim(0, L)
finish(fig, axes)
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0.02, 0, 0.82, 0.94])
plt.show()
```

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Watch this for a visual demonstration.
{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cnH2ltfW48U&start=154 >}}
:::

Notice that the frequencies in the graph, 110, 220, 330, 440 Hz, are all multiples of 110. So then, why specifically multiples?

Suppose the string has length $L$. Both ends are held fixed on the *resting line*, the straight line the string lies along when it's still, so the wave pattern has to start and end on the ends.

Starting from the resting line at the left end, the pattern only returns to it at the end of each loop. **If the string's length ended partway through a loop, the right end would be sitting above or below the line**, which is physically impossible, as the ends are fixed.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Top: a pattern with 2 loops starts and ends on the resting line, so it fits the string. Bottom: a pattern with 2.5 loops ends at a peak, leaving the right end displaced (arrow)."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(5, 4.2), sharex=True)
for ax, k in zip(axes, [2, 2.5]):
    draw_string(ax, k, nodes=np.array([0, L]))
axes[1].plot(L, 1, "o", color=COLORS[1], ms=5, zorder=3)  # where the end lands instead of 0
axes[1].annotate("", xy=(L + 0.03, 0.95), xytext=(L + 0.03, 0.05),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="k", lw=1))
axes[0].set_xlim(0, 1.06)
finish(fig, axes)
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0.02, 0, 1, 0.92])
plt.show()
```

**So a mode must contain a whole number of loops.** To write this as a formula, recall that one loop is half a wavelength. A mode with $n$ loops therefore fills the string when:

$$
L = n \cdot \frac{\lambda}{2}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\lambda = \frac{2L}{n}
$$

Even though the loops seem to stay in place, each pattern is really made of ripples running back and forth along the string, bouncing off the fixed ends. These ripples travel at one fixed speed $v$, determined by the string's tightness and weight.

For any wave, frequency is speed divided by wavelength: the faster the wave moves, or the shorter it is, the more times it vibrates each second. For mode $n$, whose wavelength is $\lambda_n = 2L/n$:

$$
f_n = \frac{v}{\lambda_n} = \frac{v}{2L/n} = n \cdot \frac{v}{2L} = n f_1,
\qquad\text{where } f_1 = \frac{v}{2L}.
$$

The speed $v$ and the length $L$ are fixed by the string, so only $n$ changes from mode to mode. For an ideal string, mode 2 therefore vibrates at exactly twice the frequency of mode 1, mode 3 at three times, and so on. (Real strings are slightly stiff, which nudges the higher harmonics a bit higher in frequency.) For our 110 Hz string, that gives 110, 220, 330 Hz.

This is also why turning a tuning peg changes the pitch: **tightening the string makes waves travel faster, which raises $v$, and with it every $f_n$**.

That settles the first question: a string can only vibrate cleanly at $f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, \ldots$. But in the rope example we only saw these patterns one at a time, each at a rhythm we chose. When we pluck a string, all these modes appear at the same time, each at a different strength. So **what's happening?**

## Where are the harmonics coming from?

In the rope example, each pattern needed its own shaking rhythm: one loop at one rhythm, two loops at twice that. But a pluck has no rhythm at all. You pull once and let go. So where do all those modes come from?

If you've seen those viral clips of a guitar string vibrating in slow, lazy waves, you might now think the rope example is exactly what a guitar string does. And now you are demanding a refund of your time from me, because if guitar vibrates like the rope, then how can there be harmonics when a wave can only vibrate at one frequency?!?!

Hear me out before you get your pitchfork. It's not quite like that. Many of those clips are filmed on a phone held inside the guitar, and those ripples are an illusion. Phone camera captures the picture line by line rather than all at once, so different parts of the string are photographed at slightly different moments.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Watch this video at 01:46 to see the illusion.
{{< video https://youtu.be/sYdXa_yp0fc?si=hYVm48Ne-3fn7DVE >}}
:::

So what does a plucked string really look like? Think about what your finger does. You are not shaking the string. You hook it with your finger, pull and let go. At that moment, the string forms a triangle: no longer a smooth curve, but two straight lines meeting at a corner, right where your finger is.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig.cap: "A guitar string is actually a triangle now?"
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

L, f1, h = 1.0, 110, 1.0
c = 2 * L * f1        # wave speed, from f1 = c / 2L
T = 1 / f1            # period of the fundamental

def triangle(x, p, h=1.0):
    """Initial shape of a string plucked at x = p to height h."""
    return np.interp(x, [0, p, L], [0, h, 0])


def extend(shape, s):
    """Odd, 2L-periodic extension of a shape defined on [0, L]."""
    s = np.mod(s, 2 * L)
    return np.where(s <= L, 1, -1) * shape(L - np.abs(L - s))


def string_at(shape, x, t):
    """d'Alembert solution for a string released from rest."""
    return 0.5 * (extend(shape, x - c * t) + extend(shape, x + c * t))

p = 0.2
x = np.linspace(0, L, 501)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.plot(x, triangle(x, p, h), "k", lw=2)
ax.plot([0, L], [0, 0], "ko", ms=6)
ax.annotate("your finger", (p, h), (p + 0.12, 0.95 * h), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->"))
ax.set(xlabel="position along string", ylabel="displacement", ylim=(-0.1, 1.2 * h))
plt.show()
```

That corner is the key to unlocking the mystery behind harmonics. To see why, we first need a closer look at how a mode moves.

A mode only ever gets taller, shorter, or flipped upside down. Freeze it at any moment and you'll see the same curve, just scaled. But at the end, it must return back to how it started. Therefore, **a mode at any moment is a scaled version of its initial and final displacement.** A sine wave is the only curve that has this special property.

:::{.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Why only a sine wave?
A tight string naturally wants to straighten itself because of tension. Wherever it's bent, it gets pulled toward the inside of the bend, and the sharper the bend, the harder the pull. A straight stretch feels no pull at all.

For a string to keep its shape, the pull has to be strongest where the string is farthest out and fade to nothing where it crosses the middle, so that every point reaches the resting line at the same time.

A sine wave has the special property where the bend at every position is proportional to its height. It is most sharply bent at its peaks, and perfectly straight where it crosses the line. Therefore, **the force exerted toward the resting line is proportional to the height.**
:::

However, the triangle is not a sine wave. Look at the triangle, its straight sides feel no pull at all; the only bend is at the corner. As only at a bend is a force induced, the corner should start moving while the sides wait, and the triangle should not keep its shape.

Let's test this prediction by releasing two strings side by side: one shaped like mode 3, and one shaped like the triangle.

```{python}
#|echo: false
#|fig.cap: "Both strings over one full period of the open A string. The dashed line is each string's starting position."
def animate_release(shapes, n_frames=60, interval=80):
    """Animate one period of motion for each initial shape in `shapes`."""
    xs = np.linspace(0, L, 501)
    times = np.linspace(0, T, n_frames, endpoint=False)
    Y = [string_at(f, xs, times[:, None]) for f in shapes.values()]  # each (n_frames, 501)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(shapes), figsize=(9, 3), sharey=True, dpi=80)
    lines = []
    for ax, (title, f), y in zip(axes, shapes.items(), Y):
        ax.plot(xs, f(xs), color="grey", lw=1, ls="--", label="starting shape")
        lines.append(ax.plot(xs, y[0], "k", lw=2.2, label="string now")[0])
        ax.set(xlim=(0, L), ylim=(-1.15, 1.15), xlabel="position along string")
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10, loc="left")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("displacement")
    axes[-1].legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="lower left")
    clock = fig.suptitle("", fontsize=10)
    fig.tight_layout()

    def draw(i):
        for line, y in zip(lines, Y):
            line.set_ydata(y[i])
        clock.set_text(f"{times[i] * 1e3:.2f} ms after release")

    anim = FuncAnimation(fig, draw, frames=n_frames, interval=interval)
    plt.close(fig)
    return anim

shapes = {
    "start as a sine":     lambda s: np.sin(3 * np.pi * s / L),
    "start as a triangle": lambda s: triangle(s, p, h),
}
HTML(animate_release(shapes).to_jshtml(default_mode="loop"))
```

The sine string behaves exactly as predicted: it only ever gets taller, shorter, or flipped. However, when the triangle is let go, its corner splits into two that run off in opposite directions, and the straight parts only start moving once a corner reaches them. Freeze it at any moment and you'll see a different shape, not a scaled triangle.

But also, watch the clock. After exactly one period, about 9.1 ms, the two corners have bounced off the ends and met again where they started, and the triangle is back to its original shape.

So the triangle isn't a mode, yet its motion repeats at exactly the fundamental's rhythm. That is a hint of what the triangle is.

## Fourier Series

For some bookkeeping, we would introduce a few formula.

Suppose we pluck the string at position $p$, pulling it up to height $h$. The starting shape is a triangle (as shown in the demonstration before):

$$
\text{triangle}(x) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{h\,x}{p}, & 0 \le x \le p \\[1.5ex]
\dfrac{h\,(L - x)}{L - p}, & p < x \le L
\end{cases}
$$

Recall that each mode is a sine wave with $n$ loops. The starting shape can be described as below:

$$
X_n(x) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
$$

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation of the shape formula:

:::

In the 1750s, Daniel Bernoulli proposed that the motion of a string fixed at both ends is a sum of its modes. Not everyone was convinced. Euler and d'Alembert objected: how could smooth sine waves ever add up to a shape with a sharp corner, like a plucked string? 

In the early 1800s, while studying how heat spreads, Joseph Fourier made an even bolder claim. He proposed that **any shape can be written as a sum of sines, including our triangle**. Mathematicians now call this a Fourier series.

$$
\text{triangle}(x) = b_1 \sin\!\left(\frac{\pi x}{L}\right) + b_2 \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi x}{L}\right) + b_3 \sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right) + \cdots = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n \sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)
$$

Each $b_n$ describes how much of mode $n$ is in the triangle. In our case, we would like to find the different modes that together construct our triangle.

To find one of them, say $b_3$, we need to isolate the third mode from all the others. We do this by exploiting a property of modes called *orthogonality*. 

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What is orthogonality?
Take two functions $f$ and $g$ on the string, $0 \le x \le L$. Multiply their values at each point along the string, then add up all the results. This gives a single number, called the *inner product* $\langle f, g \rangle$, defined as the integral $\langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^L f(x)\,g(x)\,dx$. If $\langle f, g \rangle = 0$, we say $f$ and $g$ are *orthogonal*.

The modes are orthogonal to each other: for two different modes, the positive and negative products cancel out exactly when added up. A mode paired with itself gives $\langle X_n, X_n \rangle = L/2$.

For those familiar with linear algebra, this is the dot product $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum_i u_i v_i$, applied to functions. As an exercise, you can show that the continuous functions on $[0, L]$ form a vector space, and that $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ behaves like a dot product.
:::

Due to this special property, if we multiply the whole sum by $\sin\!\left(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\right)$ and add up the result along the string, every term except the third adds up to zero:

$$
\langle \text{triangle}, X_3 \rangle = b_3 \langle X_3, X_3 \rangle
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
b_3 = \frac{\langle \text{triangle}, X_3 \rangle}{\langle X_3, X_3 \rangle} = \frac{\langle \text{triangle}, X_3 \rangle}{L/2}
$$

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## An analogy in vector spaces.
Let $\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$. They are orthonormal: $\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_j = 0$ for $i \neq j$, and $\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{e}_i = 1$. Any vector can be written as $\mathbf{v} = v_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + v_2 \mathbf{e}_2 + v_3 \mathbf{e}_3$, where $v_1, v_2, v_3$ are the scalar multiples.

We can recover $v_2$ by taking the dot product with $\mathbf{e}_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{e}_2 &= v_1 (\mathbf{e}_1 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) + v_2 (\mathbf{e}_2 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) + v_3 (\mathbf{e}_3 \cdot \mathbf{e}_2) \\
                              &= v_1 (0) + v_2 (1) + v_3 (0) = v_2
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

The same trick works for every mode, so we can find each $b_n$ one at a time:

$$
b_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L \varphi(x)\,\sin\!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)dx 
$$

Solving the integral numerically, we can now find out what are the different modes that contribute to our triangle.

## Simulating the harmonics

Here are the first 16 mode for a string plucked a quarter of the way along, each scaled by its $b_n$. The black line is the triangle we want to build:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The first 16 modes for a string plucked at 0.25, each scaled by its $b_n$. The black line is the triangle."
N_MAX = 16
MODES = np.array([np.sin(n * np.pi * x / L) for n in range(1, N_MAX + 1)])  # row n-1 = mode n
tab20 = plt.cm.tab20.colors
COLORS = list(tab20[0::2]) + list(tab20[1::2])     # 10 strong colours, then 10 lighter ones

def coefficients(p, h=h):
    """b_n for n = 1..N_MAX by numerical integration; numerical noise set to exactly 0."""
    y0 = triangle(x, p, h)
    b = np.array([2 / L * integrate(y0 * mode, x) for mode in MODES])
    b[np.abs(b) < 1e-6] = 0.0
    return b


def b_exact(n, p, h=h):
    """Exact b_n from the hand-derived formula. Accepts an array of mode numbers."""
    return 2 * h * L**2 / (np.pi**2 * n**2 * p * (L - p)) * np.sin(n * np.pi * p / L)


def partial_sum(p, N, xs, chunk=500):
    """First N modes added together at the points xs, using exact b_n.
    Built 500 modes at a time so memory stays small even for N = 10,000."""
    total = np.zeros_like(xs)
    for start in range(1, N + 1, chunk):
        n = np.arange(start, min(start + chunk, N + 1))[:, None]
        total += (b_exact(n, p) * np.sin(n * np.pi * xs / L)).sum(axis=0)
    return total


def plot_modes(ax, p):
    """Each mode scaled by its b_n, drawn high to low so mode 1 ends up on top."""
    b = coefficients(p)
    for n in reversed(range(N_MAX)):
        if b[n]:
            ax.plot(x, b[n] * MODES[n], color=COLORS[n], lw=1.6)
    ax.plot(x, triangle(x, p), color="k", lw=1)
    ax.axhline(0, color="0.6", lw=0.6)
    ax.set_xlim(0, L)


def plot_partials(ax, p, lw=1.2):
    """Running totals: curve N is the first N modes added together."""
    partials = np.cumsum(coefficients(p)[:, None] * MODES, axis=0)
    for n, y in enumerate(partials):
        ax.plot(x, y, color=COLORS[n], lw=lw)
    ax.plot(x, triangle(x, p), color="k", lw=1.5, zorder=0, label="exact triangle")
    ax.set_xlim(0, L); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.2)


def plot_many_modes(ax, p, xs, Ns):
    """Partial sums for each N in Ns, with the exact triangle drawn thinly on top."""
    for N, c in zip(Ns, COLORS):
        ax.plot(xs, partial_sum(p, N, xs), color=c, lw=1.4, label=f"{N:,} modes")
    ax.plot(xs, triangle(xs, p), color="k", lw=0.6, zorder=3, label="exact triangle")
    ax.set_xlim(xs[0], xs[-1])
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The first 16 mode for a string plucked at 0.25, each scaled by its $b_n$. The black line is the triangle."
p_single = 0.25
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))

plot_modes(ax, p_single)
ax.set(xlabel="position along string", ylabel="displacement of string")

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The fundamental, the blue hump, is the largest, but it peaks in the middle of the string, not at the pluck point. This where the other modes, or harmonics come into play.

The 2nd mode, in orange, is much smaller. It is positive on the left half and negative on the right, so it pushes the shape up near the pluck point and down on the far side. The third mode is smaller again, and the higher harmonics shrink quickly. By the 16th they are barely visible.

Now let see what happens if we add the modes one at a time. Every curve below adds one more mode to the curve before it. We should see that it starts converging into a triangle shape.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Each curve adds one more mode to the curve before it. The black line is the exact triangle."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3))

plot_partials(ax, p_single, lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="position along string", ylabel="displacement of string")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="upper right")

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The fundamental alone is a poor match for the triangle, but adding the 2nd mode pulls the peak towards the pluck point. Every mode after that makes a smaller adjustment, which slowly pulls the string to the side of the triangle.

The last part to form is the corner. Even with 16 modes, the peak is still slightly rounded. Whereas the smooth sides of the triangle need only a few modes, the sharp corner needs many high modes working together. This was the heart of Euler and d'Alembert's objection: no finite number of smooth sine waves can ever make a perfectly sharp corner. 

But Fourier's answer is that **you never have to stop**. We only have to keep adding more and more modes.

But $b_n$ also depend on where the string is plucked. Change where you pluck and you change how much of each mode contributes to the triangle. 

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Adding modes 1 to 16 for three pluck points. Plucked in the middle, the curves settle almost immediately. Plucked near the end, many high modes are needed before the sharp corner forms."
pluck_points = [0.5, 0.75, 0.95]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7, 7), sharex=True)

for ax, pp in zip(axes, pluck_points):
    plot_partials(ax, pp, lw=1.4)
    ax.set_title(f"plucked at {pp}", fontsize=10, loc="left")

axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="upper right")
axes[1].set_ylabel("displacement of string")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("position along string")

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

You can try this right now at your guitar! 

Pluck an open string right next to the bridge and you get a harsh, pinched, twangy "eeee". The reason being that pluck point excites lots of high harmonics as the sharp corner is at the end of the string, just like the bottom panel shows. The fundamental carries a smaller share of the shape, and the higher harmonics carry much more, which together forms harshness.

Now pluck the same string over the 12th fret, exactly halfway along. As every even harmonics has a note at the middle of the string, there is barely any even harmonics. The sound is dominated by the fundamental with little odds harmonics, and the curves settle onto the triangle almost immediately: this leads to a softer, rounder, hollow sound.

But let's take Fourier's advice to heart and take the sum to infinity. While we cannot compute the sum to infinite modes, we can compute it until a large enough value:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Adding 100, 1,000 and 10,000 modes for three pluck points. At original size the curves are indistinguishable from the triangle; Right side shows the triangle corner zoomed (25x)."
Ns = [100, 1000, 10000]
x_full = np.linspace(0, L, 2001)
half_width = 0.01

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(10, 8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [2, 1]})
for (ax_full, ax_zoom), pp in zip(axes, pluck_points):
    x_zoom = np.linspace(pp - half_width, pp + half_width, 4001)   
    plot_many_modes(ax_full, pp, x_full, Ns)
    plot_many_modes(ax_zoom, pp, x_zoom, Ns)
    ax_full.axvspan(x_zoom[0], x_zoom[-1], color="0.88", zorder=-1)
    ax_full.set_ylim(0, 1.1)
    ax_full.set_title(f"plucked at {pp}", fontsize=10, loc="left")
    ax_zoom.set_ylim(0.959, 1.003)
    ax_zoom.set_title("zoom on the corner", fontsize=10, loc="left")
axes[0, 1].legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="lower center")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("displacement of string")
for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("position along string")
fig.suptitle(f"Adding {Ns[0]:,} to {Ns[-1]:,} modes for three pluck points", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

All it takes is just 10,000 modes and we are pretty much exact.

At full size, the three curves are indistinguishable from the triangle. The only place they differ is the corner, so the panels on the right zoom in on it. With 100 modes the corner is still visibly rounded. With 1,000, there is only a small ripple . With 10,000 the curve is essentially indistinguishible.

So that settles the old argument. Euler and d'Alembert were right that no finite number of smooth sine waves can make a perfectly sharp corner. But Fourier was right too: we just need infinite of them. By adding enough modes, we can get as close to the corner as we like.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Are there really infinite modes when we pluck a string?
Short answer, no. Long answer, it's possible but no.


:::
